highlights:
Nvidia AI servers up 15%+, H100 rental up 40% in a year. How can enterprises lock in compute costs amid the surge? Three approaches compared.

## 1. The Price Hike Is Real: What Happened?

On August 22, 2026, Bloomberg reported that Nvidia has notified its largest customers — including Microsoft, Google, and Oracle — that servers powered by its next-generation AI chips will see price increases of over 15%, with some configurations nearing 17%. The new prices take effect for early 2027 shipments of Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell systems.

Key figures:

- H100 one-year rental climbed from $1.70/GPU/hour (Oct 2025) to $2.35 — a 38% increase
- H200 rental now at $3.50/GPU/hour
- 8x H200 server monthly rental: ~$11,500 USD
- RTX 4090 scalped to ~$7,000 on secondary markets
- On-demand GPU capacity essentially sold out globally; high-end cards backordered into 2028

The primary driver is memory. Per TrendForce, Q1 2026 DRAM contract prices surged 90-95% quarter-over-quarter, with another 58-63% increase expected in Q2. The big three memory makers are shifting capacity to HBM, creating a severe shortage of standard DRAM.

results.title: CoreWeave Tests The Limits Of Cloud Pricing - TalkMarkets
highlights:
CoreWeave leveraged surging AI demand to hike cloud pricing by 25%, signaling strong pricing power in a supply-constrained market.

The standard worry about renting out computing power is that it eventually becomes a commodity business. You buy expensive servers, you rent them out, and over time your margins get squeezed between rising hardware costs and customers demanding cheaper rates. CoreWeave CRWV is showing that the current artificial intelligence infrastructure market is behaving differently. The company raised prices across its cloud offerings by about 25% in July as near term capacity remained effectively sold out, while also saying it is passing through higher component costs. That is meaningful evidence of pricing power today. The open question is whether that power lasts once supply catches up and customers have more alternatives.

...

CoreWeave disclosed on its August earnings call that it raised prices across its cloud offerings by about 25% in July. Management said the move reflected the current demand environment and the improving returns customers are seeing as more workloads shift to inference. Separately, customers have reportedly been told that prices for some Nvidia based artificial intelligence server systems shipping early next year will rise by more than 15%. Nvidia has not publicly confirmed those increases.

...

This weakens the traditional commodity hardware argument, but it does not eliminate it. CoreWeave’s current pricing suggests that scarce near term capacity gives the company leverage when negotiating new contracts. Truist (TFC) estimates that the pricing dynamic could lift contribution margins on future longer duration deals from about 24% to about 33%. That is meaningful, but it is a deal level estimate, not a nine percentage point increase in CoreWeave’s companywide operating margin.

results.title: Nvidia to hike prices by 15%, on top of an even larger increase in July | Network World
highlights:
On top of July’s 30% price hikes across almost all of its product lines, Nvidia is reportedly preparing to raise prices of servers, including those powered by Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell chips, by 15%, due to skyrocketing memory prices.

That 15% increase for systems being delivered in early 2027, reported by Bloomberg and other business media, is seen as part of a series of expected price hikes throughout AI deployments.

...

But not all AI-related costs are increasing; per-token prices appear to be dropping, he said. That gives CIOs a potential strategy to manage costs by pushing approaches that will reduce the reliance on memory.

“The workload cost is going down per token while the underlying hardware and infrastructure costs are going up,” Bickley said. “If you are directly building out your own clusters, this is an automatic uplift to an already egregiously expensive solution. If you are buying your own hardware, you’re going to have to suck it up. You are not going to negotiate your way out of this.”

...

Gaurav Gupta, VP analyst at Gartner, noted that the Nvidia price hikes are reflective of the many pricing increases throughout the AI environment. 

“Memory prices are going up, especially HBM and LPDDR5, but there are other aspects, like leading-edge foundry wafers, advanced packaging, and other component shortages,” Gupta said, adding that those issues generate “longer lead-times, which typically translates to higher prices.” And he does not expect the situation to improve any time soon. 

“In the current environment of strong demand and limited supply, we expect this situation to continue in the near to mid-term,” he said. “This means higher costs for those deploying these servers/systems and for those renting compute in the cloud, including software vendors/model builders, and others.”

results.title: ISSUE #7: The B300 Trickle
highlights:
The one-line read. The four public floors did not move this week: H100 SXM $3.85, H200 $4.29, B200 $6.69, A100 SXM4 $2.30, the same levels we have shown since mid-July. Two things moved around them. The OCPI transaction index rose under three of the four floors, narrowing every gap on the board. And the B300, a chip that has been shipping since last year, is still finding a public price: only a few clouds list it on-demand, intermittently, and where they do the numbers range from about $7.85 to about $26.15 per GPU-hour. A settled floor, a firming index underneath it, and an established Blackwell GPU whose public price is still a trickle.

...

- Floors held. All four board floors are unchanged: H100 SXM $3.85 (Nebius), H200 $4.29 (Crusoe), B200 $6.69 (Lambda), A100 SXM4 $2.30 (Crusoe), the same levels we have published since mid-July. Across all nine indexed providers, no comparable public on-demand rate moved more than 1% week over week.
- The index moved under them. The floors held, but the OCPI transaction index did not. Week over week it rose for H100 ($2.64 to $2.87), B200 ($5.93 to $6.64), and A100 SXM4 ($1.02 to $1.07), and fell for H200 ($4.75 to $4.42). With the floors flat, every gap on the board narrowed. B200’s floor is now just $0.05 above the index, the tightest spread on the board.
- The B300 trickle. The B300 is an established Blackwell-generation GPU, in market since last year, with prior history in the AIForge Works catalog. What is still catching up is its public price. Only a handful of clouds list it on-demand, and they do so intermittently: AWS’s eight-GPU p6-b300.48xlarge appeared in Seoul for the first time in our reviewed history this week (Linux and four licensed operating-system variants), while Nebius listings dropped and then returned. We now see publicly listed on-demand B300 rates from three providers, AWS, OCI, and Nebius; CoreWeave shows the SKU but its rate is still contact-sales. The listed rates disagree sharply, from about $7.85 per GPU-hour (Nebius, three regions) to about $26.15 (AWS, Seoul). That is catalog visibility, not orderable capacity, and it is what a chip still finding its public price looks like.

...

The public catalog rates AIForge Works presents are on-demand and normalized to a per-GPU-hour basis unless stated otherwise. OCPI is transaction-index context, not a catalog price. Listed or indexed does not mean orderable, and neither is a live quote, an availability guarantee, or a purchase recommendation. Verify current pricing, availability, terms, and fees directly with the provider before acting.
